Les mitochondries tirent l'énergie du gl: Mitochondria draw energy from glucose and oxygen and store it as ATP: they are the cell's power plants. They make nothing from nothing; they slowly burn what you eat with the air you breathe.

The idea, sketched by Konstantin Mereschkowski in 1905, was defended with evidence by Lynn Margulis in 1967. The clues: mitochondria have their own DNA, circular like bacterial DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes, and divide on their own. Chloroplasts, for their part, descend from cyanobacteria.

Trois constats suffisent. Les individus: Three observations are enough. Individuals of a species vary. Part of that variation is passed on to offspring. And not all survive or reproduce equally. So, generation after generation, the variations that help leave offspring become more common. That is natural selection, published by Charles Darwin in 1859 in On the Origin of Species.
Alfred Russel Wallace avait eu la même i: Alfred Russel Wallace had had the same idea; their two texts were read together at the Linnean Society of London in 1858. Mutations, the source of variation, happen at random; selection owes nothing to chance. And "survival of the fittest" means reproductive success, not strength: an antibiotic-resistant bacterium is "fit" simply because it survives the treatment.

Version darwinienne : parmi les girafes,: The Darwinian version: among giraffes, some were born with slightly longer necks; if that helped them survive and reproduce, they left more offspring. Evolution acts on populations, over generations, never on an individual during its life. And it has no goal: some parasites have even lost organs over time.
Humains et chimpanzés : un ancêtre commu: Humans and chimpanzees: a common ancestor 6 to 7 million years ago. Birds are dinosaurs.

Les fossiles racontent ces embranchement: Fossils tell the story of these branchings. Tiktaalik, discovered in 2004, shows a transitional form between fish and four-legged animals. De 1856 à 1863, dans le jardin de son ab: From 1856 to 1863, in the garden of his abbey in Brno, the monk Gregor Mendel crossed about 28,000 plants, mostly peas. He crossed yellow and green peas: the first generation was all yellow. But in the next generation green came back, in about a quarter of the plants.
Il en déduit que chaque caractère dépend: He deduced that each trait depends on two "factors", one from each parent: our genes. He presented them in 1865, published them in 1866, and nobody took any notice. In 1900 three botanists, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, rediscovered his laws independently. Genetics was born, thirty-five years late.

In 1628 William Harvey did a simple calculation, with deliberately low estimates: in one day the heart pumps far more than the body's weight. The liver cannot produce that. Blood must therefore go round in a closed circuit.
Le cœur est une double pompe. La partie: The heart is a double pump. The right side sends blood to the lungs, the pulmonary circulation, where it picks up oxygen in about 70 m² of alveoli. The left side sends it round the whole body, the systemic circulation. And blood is never blue: it is dark red in the veins; it is the skin that makes them look blue.

Les reins font le tri : ils filtrent env: The kidneys do the sorting: they filter about 180 litres of blood a day and pass only a small part of it as urine. The pancreas produces insulin, which lets sugar into the cells; its discovery in 1921 by Banting and Best transformed the lives of diabetics.

In 1543 Andreas Vesalius published the Fabrica, illustrated with magnificent plates. He dissected human bodies, which was rare, and corrected Galen on many points: the lower jaw is a single bone, not two; the wall between the ventricles has no hole.

And no, we do not use only 10 % of our brain: imaging shows every area is used.
Bactéries et virus, deux ennemis différe: Bacteria and viruses, two different enemies
Bactérie = cellule vivante ; virus = par: Bacterium = living cell; virus = cell parasite. Antibiotics: bacteria only (Fleming, 1928).
Une bactérie est une cellule vivante, qu: A bacterium is a living cell that feeds and divides on its own. A virus is just a genetic message in a shell: it has to get into a cell and hijack its machinery to copy itself. That difference decides the treatment.
Les antibiotiques attaquent des mécanism: Antibiotics attack mechanisms specific to bacteria; against a virus, a cold or flu, they do nothing. In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday and found a culture dish overrun by a mould, Penicillium, around which the bacteria had died: that was penicillin. In his Nobel lecture in 1945 he was already warning: misused, it would make microbes resistant.

The word vaccine comes from this, from the Latin vacca, cow. Before him, people practised variolation, a risky inoculation with smallpox itself.
Le principe : présenter au système immun: The principle: show the immune system a fragment or a harmless version of the microbe. It makes antibodies and keeps a memory, which lets it react fast at the real encounter. When enough people are immune, the microbe stops circulating and protects those who cannot be vaccinated. Smallpox, declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980, remains the only human disease beaten this way.
Les antibiotiques sélectionnent les bact: Antibiotics select resistant bacteria. No antibiotic against a virus.
Une bactérie se divise parfois toutes le: A bacterium sometimes divides every twenty minutes. In an infection there are billions, and a few carry by chance a mutation that makes them resistant to an antibiotic. The treatment kills the others; the resistant ones survive and multiply. That is natural selection, before our eyes.
Producteurs → consommateurs → décomposeu: Producers → consumers → decomposers. About 10 % of the energy passes from one link to the next (Lindeman, 1942).
Une chaîne alimentaire part des producte: A food chain starts with the producers, plants and algae, which build their matter from light, water and CO₂. Then come the consumers, herbivores then carnivores, and finally the decomposers, fungi and bacteria, which return dead matter to the soil. Without them the cycles would stop.
À chaque maillon, la plus grande partie: At each link, most of the energy is lost, mainly through respiration: roughly only 10 % passes to the next level. This 10 % rule comes from Raymond Lindeman, in 1942. That is why it takes a lot of grass to feed a few gazelles, and a lot of gazelles for one lion: large predators are bound to be rare.
La matière se recycle, l'énergie vient d: Matter is recycled; energy comes from the Sun and dissipates. Natural greenhouse effect, strengthened by our emissions (Arrhenius, 1896).
La matière circule en cycles : le carbon: Matter moves in cycles: carbon goes from the air to plants, animals, soil, oceans, and back. Water evaporates, falls, runs off. Energy does not go round: it arrives from the Sun and ends up dissipated as heat.
L'effet de serre est naturel et vital :: The greenhouse effect is natural and vital: without it the Earth would be frozen. But the CO₂ we emit reinforces it. Svante Arrhenius calculated its effect as early as 1896. The oceans absorb about a quarter of our CO₂ emissions, which acidifies them, and overheated corals expel the algae that feed them: they bleach.
L'espèce qui tient tout: The species that holds it all
Espèce clé de voûte : son retrait boulev: Keystone species: removing it upsets the ecosystem (Paine, 1969). Yellowstone wolves, 1995: trophic cascade.
Certaines espèces pèsent bien plus que l: Some species weigh far more than their numbers. In the 1960s, on the coast of Washington State, the ecologist Robert Paine removed the starfish Pisaster from a stretch of shore: mussels, freed from their predator, took over everything, and the rock pools went from 15 species to 8 in three years. In 1969 he coined the term keystone species.
Le loup de Yellowstone, réintroduit en 1: The Yellowstone wolf, reintroduced in 1995, is the famous example: by keeping elk in check, it is said to have let willows and aspens grow back along the rivers. That is a trophic cascade, although its real extent is still debated. Conversely, an invasive species, like the rabbit in Australia, can throw everything off balance.
PCR : chauffer, refroidir, recopier ; ch: PCR: heat, cool, copy; each cycle doubles the DNA (30 cycles ≈ 1 billion). Mullis, 1983.
La PCR copie un fragment d'ADN des milli: PCR copies a piece of DNA billions of times. Each cycle heats the DNA to around 95 °C to separate its two strands, cools it so that small primers attach, then lets an enzyme rebuild the missing strands at around 72 °C. Each cycle doubles the number of copies: after 30 cycles, a single molecule has produced over a billion.
L'astuce : une enzyme qui résiste à la c: The trick: a heat-resistant enzyme, Taq polymerase, taken from a hot-spring bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, notably from Yellowstone. Kary Mullis invented the method in 1983 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. Diagnostic tests, criminal investigations, ancient DNA: it is everywhere.
CRISPR-Cas9 : un ARN guide mène Cas9 cou: CRISPR-Cas9: a guide RNA leads Cas9 to cut DNA at a precise spot (Charpentier and Doudna, 2012; Nobel 2020).
Les bactéries gardent en mémoire des mor: Bacteria keep pieces of DNA from viruses that have attacked them, so they can recognise and cut them up at the next attack. In 2012 Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna turned this system into a tool: a guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to a chosen sequence, where it cuts the DNA.
C'est un ciseau programmable, bien plus: It is programmable scissors, far simpler and cheaper than earlier methods. They received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. This is not biologists' first ethical debate: as early as 1975, at Asilomar, they imposed a moratorium on themselves for the first genetic manipulations.
Le vaccin qui donne une recette: The vaccine that hands over a recipe
Vaccin à ARN : une recette de protéine,: mRNA vaccine: a protein recipe, read outside the nucleus, broken down within days. Does not alter DNA (Karikó and Weissman, Nobel 2023).
Un vaccin à ARN messager ne contient pas: An mRNA vaccine does not contain the virus, but the recipe for one of its proteins. Cells read this message, make the protein, and the immune system learns to recognise it. The RNA stays outside the nucleus, where the DNA is, and breaks down within a few days: it does not alter the genome.
Cette technique n'est pas née avec la co: This technique was not born with covid-19. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found in the 2000s how to make injected RNA less inflammatory; they received the Nobel Prize in 2023. Another milestone: since 1982, insulin for diabetics has been produced by genetically modified bacteria, no longer extracted from animal pancreases.
Un malade prend un remède et guérit. Le: A patient takes a remedy and gets better. Did the remedy work? Impossible to say: they might have recovered on their own. To find out, you compare two similar groups, drawn by lot: one gets the treatment, the other a placebo, a pill with no active ingredient. Only the difference between the two counts. The ancestor of these trials dates from 20 May 1747: aboard HMS Salisbury, the Scottish doctor James Lind split twelve sailors with scurvy across six treatments. The two given oranges and lemons were almost recovered by the end of the month.
En double aveugle, ni les patients ni le: In a double-blind trial, neither patients nor doctors know who receives what, so that their expectations do not skew the result. Random allocation took hold with the British streptomycin trial against tuberculosis, published in 1948, where the statistician Austin Bradford Hill had it adopted. And a result only really counts when other teams find it again: that is reproducibility. Even a peer-reviewed article can be corrected or retracted later.
Le noyau garde l'ADN, la recette de tout: The nucleus keeps the DNA, the recipe for every protein. To make a protein, the cell copies the gene it needs into messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus. Ribosomes read this message three letters at a time and assemble the amino acids in the right order. This one-way flow, from DNA to RNA to protein, was called the "central dogma" of molecular biology by Francis Crick in 1958; he returned to it in 1970 in Nature.
Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck pensait que les: Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck thought organs change through use and that those changes are passed on: the giraffe would have lengthened its neck by stretching it, and bequeathed it to its young. He set it out in 1809 in his Zoological Philosophy, one of the first scientific theories of evolution. That is wrong: a muscular blacksmith does not have more muscular children. What you acquire in your life is not written into your genes.
Deux parents Aa : chacun transmet A ou a: Two Aa parents: each passes on A or a, at random. The table gives AA, Aa, aA and aa. This grid bears the name of the English geneticist Reginald Punnett, who devised it around 1905, shortly after Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900. On average one child in four is aa and shows the recessive trait. Careful: dominant does not mean common. Polydactyly, having extra fingers, is dominant and yet rare.
D'où les règles : ne pas prendre d'antib: Hence the rules: do not take antibiotics against a virus, and finish the prescribed course, so as not to let the toughest bacteria survive. Alexander Fleming, who had discovered penicillin in 1928, was already warning in 1945, in his Nobel lecture: he feared that "the ignorant man" would underdose himself. Fever is not the enemy: it hinders the growth of some microbes and activates the defences.
